--- title: Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis description: This chapter delves into the techniques of bivariate and multivariate analysis, which are essential for understanding relationships between multiple variables in a dataset. author: Md Muztahid Hassan date: '2026-05-09 23:00:00' toc: true execute: warning: false echo: true order: 7 --- ## Bivariate Analysis Bivariate analysis involves examining the relationship between two variables. ## Multivariate Analysis Multivariate analysis involves examining the relationships among three or more variables. Here are some common techniques for both types of analysis: We will use titanic, tips, iris, and flights datasets for our examples. ::: {#758d1086 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import seaborn as sns import pandas as pd titanic = sns.load_dataset('titanic') tips = sns.load_dataset('tips') flights = sns.load_dataset('flights') iris = sns.load_dataset('iris') ``` ::: ## 1. Scatterplot (Numerical - Numerical) If we want to analyze the relationship between two numerical variables: total_bill and tip, we can use a scatterplot. ::: {#cdfa29de .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} tips.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
total_bill tip sex smoker day time size
0 16.99 1.01 Female No Sun Dinner 2
1 10.34 1.66 Male No Sun Dinner 3
2 21.01 3.50 Male No Sun Dinner 3
3 23.68 3.31 Male No Sun Dinner 2
4 24.59 3.61 Female No Sun Dinner 4
``` ::: ::: ::: {#2fb0a292 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x='total_bill', y='tip') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=585 height=429} ::: ::: Let's say we want to know the male and female status of customers in the scatterplot. We can use the hue parameter to differentiate between them. > In this case, we can say that it is a multivariate analysis because we are analyzing the relationship between three variables: total_bill, tip, and sex. ::: {#347b42ea .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x='total_bill', y='tip', hue='sex') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=585 height=429} ::: ::: If we want to find who are the smokers and non-smokers in the scatterplot, we can use the style parameter. ::: {#3b1ca32e .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x='total_bill', y='tip', hue='sex', style='smoker') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=585 height=429} ::: ::: ## 2. Bar plot (Numerical - Categorical) If we want to analyze the relationship between a numerical variable and a categorical variable, we can use a bar plot. We will use the titanic dataset for this example. ::: {#70a00366 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} titanic.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
survived pclass sex age sibsp parch fare embarked class who adult_male deck embark_town alive alone
0 0 3 male 22.0 1 0 7.2500 S Third man True NaN Southampton no False
1 1 1 female 38.0 1 0 71.2833 C First woman False C Cherbourg yes False
2 1 3 female 26.0 0 0 7.9250 S Third woman False NaN Southampton yes True
3 1 1 female 35.0 1 0 53.1000 S First woman False C Southampton yes False
4 0 3 male 35.0 0 0 8.0500 S Third man True NaN Southampton no True
``` ::: ::: ::: {#56b40b4e .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.barplot(data=titanic, x = "pclass", y = "age", hue = "sex") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=585 height=429} ::: ::: ## 3. Box plot (Numerical - Categorical) We will use the same titanic dataset for this example. ::: {#c9c307ab .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.boxplot(data = titanic, x = "pclass", y = "age", hue = "survived") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=585 height=429} ::: ::: ## 4. Kdeplot (Numerical - Categorical) We will use the same titanic dataset for this example. ::: {#5d2cfd49 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.kdeplot(data = titanic, x = "age", hue = "survived", fill = True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=614 height=430} ::: ::: ## 5. Pairplot (Numerical - Numerical) If we want to analyze the relationship between multiple numerical variables, we can use a pairplot. We will use the iris dataset for this example. ::: {#f5d0fb04 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} iris.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
sepal_length sepal_width petal_length petal_width species
0 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2 setosa
1 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2 setosa
2 4.7 3.2 1.3 0.2 setosa
3 4.6 3.1 1.5 0.2 setosa
4 5.0 3.6 1.4 0.2 setosa
``` ::: ::: ::: {#054f9d58 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.pairplot(data = iris) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){width=947 height=947} ::: ::: ## 6. Line plot (Numerical - Numerical) We will use the flights dataset for this example. ::: {#cbe66b3c .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
year month passengers
0 1949 Jan 112
1 1949 Feb 118
2 1949 Mar 132
3 1949 Apr 129
4 1949 May 121
``` ::: ::: ::: {#f7976e05 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} new_data = flights.groupby('year', as_index=False)['passengers'].sum() new_data.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}
year passengers
0 1949 1520
1 1950 1676
2 1951 2042
3 1952 2364
4 1953 2700
``` ::: ::: ::: {#2deb9bd5 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.lineplot(data = new_data, x = 'year', y = 'passengers') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){width=601 height=429} ::: ::: > These are the manual techniques for bivariate and multivariate analysis. To automate this process, we can use the ydata-profiling library, which provides a comprehensive report of the dataset, including bivariate and multivariate analysis. ::: {#074bd37e .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport prof = ProfileReport(titanic) prof.to_file(output_file='output.html') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: This will generate an HTML file with a detailed report of the titanic dataset, including bivariate and multivariate analysis. You can open the output.html file in your browser to explore the report.
